newsitem.title: ALBANIA: More missed deadlines as Albania poll nears.
newsitem.headline: More missed deadlines as Albania poll nears.

text.p: Albania's independent election organisers have missed another deadline in preparing for a June 29 parliamentary vote, raising fears there may not even be ballot papers ready for polling day.

Mark Smith, spokesman for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, said on Tuesday a "significant proportion" of candidates' names had not reached the OSCE by Monday, 12 days before election day.

The OSCE, in Albania to assist and monitor the poll, needs candidate names to get ballot papers printed abroad. Smith also said some of Albania's 115 electoral zones had failed to tell it yet how many ballot papers they need.
"There is concern because the deadline has not been met," he said, but would not say if it would now be impossible for the OSCE to provide the ballot papers.

Tensions are mounting as Albania lurches towards the elections, called in a bid to restore law and order after five months of anarchy and violence following the collapse of fraudulent investment schemes earlier this year.

Political parties and overseas observers insist that, for stability and calm, the poll must go ahead on the agreed date, but Albania's multi-party election organisers have already been forced to cut corners in procedure.

Thimjo Kondi, secretary of the Central Election Commission, said on Monday candidate lists were ready in some areas, like the southern town of Vlore, but roads are dangerous and no protection is on offer from multinational forces to fetch them.

A 6,500-strong Italian-led force in the country has a mandate only to protect aid convoys and overseas observers. The United Nations has not authorised it to take a security role during the elections, sparking some resentment in local press.
Voter lists, due by law to be posted around June 12 or 13, are only now starting to appear, at least in the capital, Tirana.

Kondi said problems had been compounded by a delay in the presidential decree needed to start planning for the polls and by an ambitious bid to stage a referendum, also on June 29, to decide if Albania will stay a republic or become a constitutional monarchy.
In its role as election planner, the commission has joined opposition parties and international groups in pushing for polls to close before nightfall.
The current law stipulates a 9 p.m. closure, which they have argued risks intimidation of late voters or manipulation.
"I have publicly insisted the polling stations should be closed earlier," Kondi said. "People are scared -- the night is dangerous."
The commission, at work for just over two weeks, has also had difficulties communicating instructions to some areas, but Kondi said it must keep pushing ahead.
"The credibility and the lost faith of the people needs to be restored," he said.
